title: OPEC+ Approves Sixth Straight Output Hike, Then Plans to Pause Through Year-End
excerpt: Seven OPEC+ producers will add 188,000 barrels per day in September, completing the rollback of 2023 voluntary cuts. The group then plans to freeze quotas through Q4 as it tackles the thornier question of 2027 production baselines.
body:
• OPEC+ agreed Sunday to raise output targets by 188,000 barrels per day for September, the sixth consecutive monthly increase since April.
  • The hike completes the unwinding of 1.65 million bpd in voluntary cuts agreed in 2023, adjusted for the UAE's departure from the alliance in May.
  • Quotas will be frozen from October through year-end as the group reviews production capacity to set 2027 baselines.
  • For India, which imports roughly 85% of its crude, normalized Gulf flows could ease pressure on the current account deficit and fuel inflation.

Seven OPEC+ producers led by Saudi Arabia agreed Sunday to raise their combined output target by about 188,000 barrels per day from September, according to the Wall Street Journal and Reuters, marking the sixth straight monthly increase and completing a phased rollback of supply cuts first imposed in 2023.

The decision, taken during a virtual meeting on August 2, had been widely expected. But the more consequential signal came alongside it: OPEC+ plans to pause further quota increases through the rest of 2026, freezing production targets for the fourth quarter as it turns to the contentious task of setting output baselines for 2027.

Completing the Rollback

The September increase brings to a close the unwinding of 1.65 million bpd in voluntary cuts that Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman originally agreed to in late 2023, when the group still included the UAE. The UAE left OPEC in late April, seeking to align its production more closely with its growing capacity under national oil company ADNOC.

A separate set of group-wide OPEC+ cuts totaling around 2 million bpd, introduced in 2022, will remain in place through year-end.

"OPEC+ has spent months raising targets while actual group output fell. The increases gave members permission to restore supply whenever wells, pipelines, ports, and shipping lanes allowed it. Permission was the easy part."

— OilPrice.com analysis

The Pause and the 2027 Question

Sources told Reuters that current production targets would remain in place from October until new quotas take effect in January 2027. OPEC+ is reviewing the maximum sustainable production capacity of its members, a process set to conclude by September. The results will form the basis for 2027 output baselines. Iraq and several other producers want higher quotas to reflect investments that have expanded their capacity, setting up difficult internal negotiations.

The seven producers are scheduled to meet again on September 6 to formally decide October production levels.

Paper Barrels vs. Real Barrels

The quota increases have been largely symbolic. The five-month-old U.S.-Iran conflict has disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — previously a conduit for roughly a fifth of global crude supply — and reduced actual OPEC+ output well below targets. Production fell to 33.13 million bpd in May from 42.77 million bpd in February, according to OPEC data. Output began recovering in June but remains below pre-war levels.

Oil prices ended July with their largest monthly gain since March after hostilities between the U.S. and Iran flared again. Brent crude has averaged about $87 per barrel year-to-date, a Reuters poll showed, well above pre-conflict levels near $72. On Saturday, President Trump called off a planned attack on Iran, saying "the perimeters of a deal had been agreed to" that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic.

"The key support remains the geopolitical risk premium associated with the Iran conflict, which is likely to persist through the second half of the year and keep volatility elevated."

— Tobias Keller, UniCredit analyst

India Watches Closely

India, which imports approximately 85% of its crude oil, stands to benefit if OPEC+ quotas eventually translate into real supply growth. A finance ministry report published last week warned that sustained high oil prices could strain both India's fiscal deficit and current account balance. The current supply gap has lifted India's import bill and pressured inflation — every $10-per-barrel increase in crude widens the current account deficit by roughly 0.4% of GDP, according to analysts. Normalized Gulf flows would provide fiscal breathing room heading into the second half of the fiscal year.

What's Next

HSBC's base case assumes Hormuz traffic recovering to about 80% of pre-conflict levels by end-September, with the market swinging into surplus by Q4 2026 and prices potentially falling toward $65 per barrel in 2027. The IEA projects a significant supply overhang in 2027, with global supply set to surge by 8 million bpd while demand rises by just 2 million.

For OPEC+, the immediate challenge is less about pumping more oil than about deciding who gets to pump it. With Iraq pressing for higher quotas, Kazakhstan constrained by Black Sea disruptions, and Russia dealing with refinery outages, the capacity review set to conclude next month will test the group's cohesion in ways the monthly quota increases never did.
nri_angle: India imports 85% of its crude oil; sustained high prices strain its fiscal and current account deficits, while normalized Gulf flows could ease fuel inflation.
